Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace. Squarespace: share your passion with the world. There’s an ancient Greek legend about a
ship that launched from the port of Theseus, and sailed around the world. Probably not around the WHOLE world.
Just AROUND the world. During its journey, the ship encountered many
dangers. Storms ravaged its sails, which had to be
replaced. The floorboards gradually gave way, and had
to be changed out, one by one. Eventually, crew members decided that they liked the look of some island or another along the way, and stayed behind. And as the ship sailed on, more and more of
it – and its crew – was replaced, until finally, not a single original plank
of wood, or hand on deck, remained. Now here’s the question: When the ship finally returned to Theseus, was it the same ship that left? The answer – whether we can find it or not
– lies in the concept of identity. Philosophers describe identity as the relation
that a thing bears only to itself. So, whatever makes a thing uniquely what it
is defines its identity. And if two things are identical, they’re
said to share an identity relation. Now, whether two things are the same might
seem blindingly obvious. But of course it isn’t.
Because: philosophy. The philosophy of identity can get pretty slippery, largely because, like the Ship of Theseus, things change. And when they do, they eventually stop being
what they are, and become something else. This goes not just for mythological ships,
but for all kinds of things. Like, this mug can acquire a new identity.
And this money. And you.
And even … Batman. [Theme Music] So, riddle me this:
Is Batman identical to Bruce Wayne? And when I say “identical,” I don’t
mean that they just look alike. I mean that they share the same identity – they’re
literally one and the same. So, you might think the answer is yes – Bruce Wayne and Batman are identical because everyone knows that Bruce Wayne is the man behind the cowl. Not only that, you might say: Bruce Wayne
is the very essence of Batman. He saw his parents get killed in that alley.
He became the Dark Knight. No one else could take his place. But hold up.
People have taken his place. It turns out that Dick Grayson, the original
Robin, has pinch-hit for Batman, donning the cape and cowl to protect the streets
of Gotham in his boss’s absence. And so has Police Commissioner Jim Gordon. After Bruce Wayne was reported dead, he reluctantly
accepted the role himself. Both of those guys have been Batman. So if the person inside the costume doesn’t
make Batman Batman, then what does? 17th century German philosopher Gottfried
Wilhelm Leibniz came up with a principle that might help us solve the puzzle of Who
Batman Is. He called it the Indiscernibility of Identicals. The idea is that, if any two things are identical,
then they must share all the same properties. If Leibniz is right, then the Ship of Theseus became a new ship as soon as that first plank of wood was replaced. As soon as its parts were not all original,
then the ship suddenly acquired a new property. And with a new property came a new identity. So likewise, Bruce Wayne and Batman can’t be identical, because they have different properties. Bruce Wayne, for example, has the property of being a millionaire playboy, but Batman doesn’t. That guy is all business. Meanwhile, Batman has the property of having
fought the Joker, but Bruce Wayne doesn’t. And the different versions of Batman aren’t
identical to each other either. Because the person wearing the costume, even if it’s the exact same costume – which it usually isn’t – is going to have different combat techniques,
and even, say, a different moral code. So, is there a limit to how much something
can change, and still be the same thing? Let’s head over to the Thought Bubble for
some Flash Philosophy. Think about this little puzzler, originally offered by contemporary American philosopher Alan Gibbard. A sculptor takes a lump of clay, and names
it Lumpl. She then forms Lumpl into a statue, which
she names Goliath. Are Lumpl and Goliath identical? Our intuition might say yes, because they’re composed of exactly the same amount of the same physical stuff. It’s been kneaded and molded into a different
shape, but still: No part of Lumpl is not Goliath, and no part
of Goliath is not Lumpl. But consider this: If we wreck the statue, and smush into into a big blob, Goliath is gone, because part of what it means to be Goliath
is to be shaped like a statue. But, Lumpl, being a lump, doesn’t have a
set shape. So it will remain, after Goliath has been
destroyed. So on one hand, Gibbard observed, Lumpl and
Goliath seem to be identical, because they’re the same exact thing, just
in different shapes. But on the other hand, how can Lumpl and Goliath be identical, if one can exist while the other does not? Thanks, Thought Bubble! One way to try and make sense of identity, and explain how an object endures over time, is by making a distinction between what we
call essential and accidental properties. Essential properties are the core elements
needed for a thing to be the thing that it is. Accidental properties are traits that could be taken away from an object without making it a different thing. Think about a dog.
A dog without a tail is still a dog. Give him a shave, or a silly poodle doo, don’t
let it bark – you still have a dog. So all those things are all accidental properties,
and they’re pretty easy to pick out. But it can be really tough to find its essential
properties, the things that, if they were absent,
would make the dog not a dog anymore.

###  Ship of Theseus - Philosophy Deep Dive

**Introduction:** The Ship of Theseus is a philosophical allegory exploring the concept of identity. This legendary ship embarked on a journey with eventual deterioration; replacing planks as it sailed and, by the end, no original wood remained. The essence remains in debate – did it remain the same ship? 

**The Philosophy of Identity:** In philosophy, identity relates to one's essential self. A thing's traits define its unique identity.  For example:
* Things can change over time but still hold their core identity (e.g., a ship going through various phases).
* Like anything else, the philosophical implications are vast and complex.

**Exploring Identity in Real Life:** 
* Mug – It's true; items change over time becoming something completely different, yet it has the essence of its past life: an inherent essence defining what it is now.
* Money -  Money undergoes economic transformations during storage but retains its value as a representation of wealth, even when physically altered (e.g., a crumpled coin vs. a new one).
* You – The core you remains; your experiences shape who you are despite material and environmental changes that often impact physical appearance. Even Batman—the embodiment of identity through his persona. 

**Leibniz's Indiscernibility - A Key Insight:** This principle suggests that if two things are identical, that is their defining characteristic in relation to the other thing- even they are different (e.g., a ship) or identical (like two people with similar traits).
* Ship: As soon as there was a change within its core body; it became a replacement for the original.

**Batman and Identity:** An intriguing exploration of Batmens' identity and how Bruce Wayne acts as a catalyst. Does Batman's identity become an external or a reflection of himself, which changes with context (e.g., when he is retired) – and the people involved? 
* A Bruce Wayne was found dead to show that someone else could embody this persona—both Jim Gordon and Dick Grayson in action as "Batman"

**Theories on Identity Change:** Philosophers delve into different theories of change: a focus on what stays the same. One prominent example is Alan Gibbard's observation about two clay pieces with seemingly identical composition – Lumpl and Goliath. Does one remain, while the other is transformed?

**Essential vs Accidental Properties (A philosophical approach to things):**
* Essential properties are core elements that form 'the thing'. Accidental are characteristics that aren’t crucial - the dog as a complete dog regardless of facial hair changes (e.g.,  Shaving it or getting a new haircut) and so on!

**Understanding What Is Truly "The Same"**: A deep dive into how something can remain "The Same", even through significant physical alterations or changes over time: essence and identity; what truly defines those things. 
 - Philosophical thoughts; this is a central element that ties many things together.

Identical objects are said to have an "identity relation."  While seemingly obvious, philosophy can complicate matters when things change over time.  This applies not just to ships (like in Plato's *Ship of Theseus*), but all kinds of subjects, from everyday items like mugs or money to larger entities such as Batman himself. 

The question arises: Is Bruce Wayne identical with Batman? If so, their identity is clear because everyone knows the man behind the cowl.  However, this identification doesn’t always hold true, especially considering alternate versions like Dick Grayson and Jim Gordon who've served the "Batman" role in Gotham. A significant challenge lies in pinpointing exactly what constitutes a Batman-specific defining characteristic.

German philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz advanced the principle of Indiscernibility of Identicals. In essence, if two identical objects possess all the same properties, then those characteristics encompass the entirety of their identity. 
If this is true, even subtle differences, like replacing a plank in a ship, transform it into something new, even as there are no radical structural changes.  This principle also sheds light on Bruce Wayne and Batman's relationship.  Bruce Wayne embodies particular elements - such as wealth (millionaire playboy) but not always the aggressive "Batman" persona. Conversely, Batman, though he fights villains like the Joker, holds an individuality that is absent in his human counterpart. 

The philosopher Alan Gibbard challenges us to consider another aspect of identity: what counts as fundamental properties? Does a lump of clay (Lumpl) truly become Goliath when molded? This raises questions about whether "Goliath" remains independent of its form once reshaped from the initial lump of materials, or is it a different entity.  

Some philosophers divide essential identities based on accidental traits, which are aspects that could be changed without altering the thing's identity - just think of a dog – you can shave their fur, even give them a silly haircut– and still recognize the same pet. 
This question takes us through numerous scenarios of transformations: A tree losing its leaves but still existing as a tree is one, as is changing it into paper pulp. We are left questioning what makes something remain an identity.

One method used to explain this problem of existence is through the concept of essential properties. In essence, these properties define the thing and can't be altered without impacting its definition.  Think about a dog; even if it loses its tail or has special features. It will continue to be a dog, regardless of these changes. Identifying characteristics that form the very soul of an entity can become complex: some argue their essential components exist independently from these external manifestations, while others might believe them as inseparable from each other. 

For instance, Heraclitus suggests an influential concept – "nothing is identical to itself."  In his view, everything continuously transforms; this process makes us recognize a continuous cycle of existence with constant change in every aspect of someone's life and those people’s identities. This philosophical argument compels us to confront the idea that even seemingly fixed entities are undergoing some form of evolution, which can challenge our very understanding of identity.

Defining Identity

Bruce Wayne and Batman's shared origin story has led to questions about what constitutes "Batman" when Bruce Wayne, a millionaire playboy, isn't in costume. Philosophers propose concepts to understand how identity works over time. 

Thought Bubble Exploration: Identical Objects
This discussion draws from Alan Gibbard’s puzzle of a sculptor creating two objects: Lumpl (a lump of clay) and Goliath (formed from that lump). The core dilemma arises when considering whether identical objects remain the same when their shapes change, such as moving from being a lump to a statue.  
* Are identical things necessarily different? 

Differentiated Properties: Essential and Accidental
Philosophers propose dividing properties into these categories:
    * **Essential Properties**:  Core elements defining something (like a dog's need to bark or wag its tail). Losing these would make it significantly different; consider, for example, the loss of an ear.
    * **Accidental properties** – traits that could be removed without altering the fundamental nature of something (such as the type of fur, length of tail, or color of eyes)

The Importance of Identity
